claims.claim: As of 2026-10-06, ordinary commercial low-value imports cannot rely on the former Section 321 de minimis duty-free model; appropriate entry and applicable duties/fees are required under the post-suspension regime.
claims.counterevidence: Separate statutory treatment remains for certain bona fide gifts and other narrow exceptions; suspension should not be generalized beyond its scope.

claims.claim: CBP's Entry Type 13 test demonstrates a current legal/operational path in which an owner or purchaser, or a properly appointed licensed customs broker, can make electronic informal mail entry without a comparison platform itself becoming IOR.
claims.counterevidence: Entry Type 13 is a voluntary test and its published response volumes are Paperwork Reduction Act estimates, not evidence of actual market adoption.

claims.claim: The importer-of-record boundary is a major architecture transition: qualifying owner/purchaser or licensed broker makes entry, and import duties constitute a debt of the importer.
claims.counterevidence: A broker can act as IOR in some structures and can remit duties, so payment flow alone does not identify the legal importer.

claims.claim: A platform that performs classification, valuation, admissibility or prepares customs documents for consumers risks conducting regulated customs business; mere electronic transmission of received data is expressly excluded.
claims.counterevidence: An importer conducting customs business solely for its own account does not require a broker license, and pure data transmission is outside the statutory customs-business definition.

claims.claim: CPSC responsibility changes materially when the platform becomes the commercial importer: regulated imports generally require importer certification/eFiling from July 8, 2026, while CPSC says it will not typically consider a personal-use consumer the importer responsible for certification; transport-only 3PLs also have a statutory role carve-out.
claims.counterevidence: The consumer language is 'not typically,' not an absolute exemption, and the 3PL protection applies only when the entity's role is solely receiving, holding or transporting without taking title.

claims.claim: A pure comparison/routing layer can still face FCC issues for RF devices because FCC marketing includes advertising for sale; imported SDoC equipment can make the importer the responsible party.
claims.counterevidence: FCC rules contain a narrow personal-use import exception for three or fewer devices in specified categories; whether a particular neutral comparison interface constitutes prohibited marketing is fact-dependent.

claims.claim: Physical or commercial logistics aggregation does not by itself make the platform an importer, but operating as a transportation intermediary can trigger separate regimes such as TSA indirect-air-carrier security requirements or FMC OTI/NVOCC licensing and financial responsibility.
claims.counterevidence: Using an already regulated carrier/forwarder and merely negotiating commercial rates need not make the platform itself the regulated transportation intermediary.

claims.claim: Moving into inventory/retail or a third-party marketplace creates additional obligations independent of customs status, including CPSC hazard reporting for manufacturers/importers/distributors/retailers and INFORM Act duties for qualifying online marketplaces.
claims.counterevidence: INFORM's marketplace obligations concern third-party sellers and do not by themselves turn an own-inventory retailer into a third-party marketplace.

claims.claim: Superbuy's public operating model is consistent with a shopping-agent/forwarding structure in which users direct purchases, parcels may be consolidated, and destination customs charges are described as borne by the recipient, but these public terms do not establish the actual U.S. IOR for each route.
claims.counterevidence: Actual legal status depends on carrier contracts, entry filings, broker powers of attorney and route-specific customs practices, none of which were available on the public pages reviewed.

claims.claim: A plausible light-asset architecture can obtain commercially negotiated logistics scale while keeping the consumer/qualified broker as the customs-side principal, provided the platform avoids taking title, acting as IOR, unlicensed customs brokerage, or independently operating regulated transportation services.
claims.counterevidence: No source reviewed constitutes regulatory approval of this exact business model, and particular logistics contracts may allocate title, IOR, consignee or carrier functions differently.
